prompts.L4:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Memories, Letting, What

outputs.L1:
I am not saying, “Mark my words,”  
as the thief says early each winter.  
He leaves nothing of value. He, too, wants.  
A brute with language, he has a fondness  
for preaching. I am bathed to luster.  
Memories move musically through my bones.

He sings above, vaults off a horse with feigned  
kindness, lands so fancy. Letting go of this,  
sitting with tropical leaves the size of men  
in a terrarium, I am beautiful. He means well,  
admonishing women. He is lucky  
with the show of crankiness.

What does it mean to let go of envy?  
I sometimes hope stars don’t spread themselves  
over New York’s lights. Performing for himself,  
glasses glittering, he reads stories of poverty,  
claims them all as his own.

Here in Colorado, irises of all colors unfold  
outward to the half-hidden sun. On the cracked  
cement, chilly before rain, I see perpetual beginnings.

I’m going to forget him:  
lock him in a box in my head,  
lock him in the haunt of violins,  
let go of what’s his in the hurling breath  
of my groans.
outputs.L2:
I won’t declare, “Remember what I tell you,”  
the way the burglar does at winter’s outset.  
He takes away nothing precious,  
though he is driven by desire as well.  
A creature made rough despite his gift for speech,  
he delights in delivering sermons.

I have been polished until I gleam.  
Recollections hum their way through my skeleton.  
Overhead, he sings, then springs from a horse,  
pretending gentleness  
and touching down with elaborate grace.

Releasing all of this, I sit among tropical foliage  
whose leaves are as large as people,  
enclosed inside a glass habitat,  
and I am lovely.

His intentions are good  
when he lectures women.  
Even his displayed irritability  
seems to work in his favor.

How does one surrender jealousy?  
At times I wish the stars would not scatter  
across the glow of New York City.

Putting on a performance for no one but himself,  
his spectacles flashing,  
he recites accounts of hardship  
and adopts every one as though it belonged to him.

In Colorado, irises in every shade  
open toward a sun partly concealed.  
On fractured concrete, cold in the air before rainfall,  
I recognize beginnings that never cease.

I will erase him from memory:  
seal him inside a mental container,  
confine him where violins linger like ghosts,  
and expel whatever belongs to him  
on the forceful breath of my moaning.
outputs.L3:
The speaker portrays a self-important and moralizing man who exploits others while carefully presenting himself as generous, compassionate, and well-intentioned. His apparent kindness is revealed as a performance: beneath his virtuous public image lies a willingness to take from those around him. This contradiction makes him both morally troubling and emotionally difficult for the speaker to dismiss.

Even after his absence, memories of the man remain intensely vivid. They take on a musical quality, echoing through the speaker’s mind and shaping not only their emotions but also their bodily experience. His remembered voice, gestures, and theatrical presence continue to exert influence, as though the performance has survived the performer. The speaker therefore struggles with envy, resentment, and the difficulty of releasing someone whose image has become deeply embedded in memory.

Against this artificiality, the natural landscapes of Colorado provide a powerful contrast. Images of beauty, growth, and renewal suggest a world capable of continual transformation—of “perpetual beginnings.” Nature does not depend on moral posturing or staged benevolence; its restorative power feels genuine and ongoing. Through this contrast, the speaker begins to imagine a life no longer dominated by the man’s carefully constructed persona.

Ultimately, the speaker resolves to limit his influence by confining him to the past. Although the memories cannot simply be erased, they can be contained and deprived of their power over the present. The final act of emotional forgetting is therefore not a denial that he existed, but a deliberate release: the speaker chooses to stop sustaining his performance through continued attention and to reclaim the freedom to begin again.
outputs.L4:
Here is an original poetic expansion of the summary:

---

You enter every room as though it were a stage,  
wearing borrowed colors with the confidence  
of someone who has forgotten where he found them.  
You lift other people’s stories to your mouth  
and speak them as if they began with you.  
Once, I mistook that certainty for brilliance.  
Once, I envied the ease with which the world  
turned its face toward your rehearsed light.

But I remember what existed before you:  
rain loosening the dust from summer leaves,  
the river carrying fallen branches onward,  
the patient return of green after a fire.  
None of these asked to be admired.  
None declared itself the author of morning.  
They simply continued—quiet, sufficient, free.

So I gather what remains of you:  
the applause, the old arguments,  
the sharp little relics of resentment.  
I place them in a room behind me  
and close the door without ceremony.  
You may live there among your performances,  
preserved in the tense of what has been.  
I will not carry you into another season.

Outside, the wind is already changing.  
I loosen my hands. I release what they held.  
My face returns to me, unmeasured by your gaze;  
my beauty becomes something living again—  
not a prize, not a reflection, not a debt,  
but the wild renewal of a field after winter.

Letting go is not emptiness.  
It is space: a window opened,  
a path appearing where the snow has melted.  
I step forward with nothing to prove.  
The world begins beneath my feet,  
and because I am free to leave the past behind,  
it can begin again and again.
outputs.L5:
### What We Keep

Memories are strange companions. They arrive without warning—in the scent of rain, the opening notes of an old song, or the sight of light falling across an empty room. Some bring comfort; others remind us of doors that have closed.

Letting go does not mean forgetting. It means accepting that the past cannot be changed, only carried differently. Over time, sharp edges soften. The moments that once hurt become part of a larger story, woven together with joy, loss, hope, and growth.

What remains is not always what happened, but how it shaped us. We keep the laughter, the lessons, and even the silences. Then, little by little, we make room for what comes next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about letting go of envy toward a charismatic but self-important man, contrasting New York lights with Colorado irises and ending with locking him away in memory.
counterfactuals.output:
He entered every room  
as if the room had rehearsed for him—  
all bright teeth, gravity,  
a voice polished smooth  
by its own applause.

For years I mistook his radiance  
for evidence against my own,  
counted the faces turning toward him  
like windows catching  
the New York lights—  
restless towers glittering  
as though height were holiness.

I carried envy  
like a green coin under my tongue,  
tasting metal  
whenever he spoke his name  
into the center of the world.

Then Colorado opened:  
a quieter blue,  
irises lifting from the earth  
without mirrors,  
without witnesses,  
their purple throats holding rain.

They did not ask the mountains  
to admire them.  
They did not dim  
because another flower bloomed nearby.

So I release him  
from the throne I built in secret.  
Let Manhattan keep its electric crowns,  
its brilliant windows  
burning long past sleep.

I choose the iris—  
rooted, brief,  
unconcerned with being seen.

And when his old charm knocks again,  
wearing its practiced light,  
I will close the door gently,  
turn the key,  
and lock him away in memory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal contemporary poem featuring a thief who preaches, tropical leaves in a terrarium, glittering glasses, stories of poverty, and the haunting sound of violins.
counterfactuals.output:
The thief preaches beneath a pharmacy sign,  
his pockets ringing with borrowed moons.  
He says, *Blessed are the unlocked doors,*  
and the crowd lifts its glittering glasses  
to catch the blue light of passing phones.

In the café window, a terrarium sweats—  
tropical leaves pressing green tongues  
against the glass, trying to warn us  
that paradise is always rented  
by someone who never arrives.

We trade stories of poverty like weather:  
the winter when the power vanished,  
the mother who boiled water for dinner,  
the boy who wore his brother’s shoes  
until both their footsteps disappeared.

Still, the thief keeps preaching.  
From his sleeve he releases black butterflies,  
receipts, a small red siren.  
He steals the names from every bank  
and gives them to the homeless stars.

Then the violins begin—  
not played, but remembered,  
their thin cries drifting from elevators,  
storm drains, the mouths of mannequins.  
All night they follow us home,

while the leaves breathe in their glass country  
and our glittering cups go dark,  
each holding one trembling note  
we cannot spend,  
and cannot return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical prose poem in the voice of a woman trying to forget a performative, admonishing man. Use fragmented syntax, vivid natural imagery, and an emotionally cathartic ending.
counterfactuals.output:
I try to forget him in the ordinary weather.

Rain worrying the windows. Pears softening in a blue bowl. The moon—its white mouth open, saying nothing.

Unlike him.

He stood always beneath an invisible spotlight, one hand lifted as if blessing a crowd, as if every room had gathered to witness his sorrow. Even his tenderness rehearsed. Even his silence wore a costume. He told me how to speak, how to grieve, how a woman ought to carry her anger: discreetly, like a covered dish.

No spilling. No smoke.

I became small beside him. A field after locusts. A house with all its bells removed.

Now I walk where the river shoulders through reeds, brown and swollen with spring. The willows drag their green hair in the current. Somewhere, a heron unfolds—slow hinge of heaven—and leaves no applause behind.

I practice losing him.

His sermons first. His grave, instructive eyes. The finger raised between us like a little pale tower.

Then his name.

I give it to the mud, which takes everything without judgment. I give it to the river, which does not ask what I did to deserve thirst. I give it to the wind worrying the dead grass, and the grass does not answer.

All evening, clouds bruise open over the hills.

I open, too.

Not beautifully. Not as he would have directed. I open like thunder. Like a seed split by its own furious green. Like a door kicked wide in a burning house.

And what comes out is not forgiveness.

It is breath.

Mine—ragged, animal, holy.

I breathe until the spotlight dies. Until his voice is only a moth battering itself against some distant lamp. Until morning climbs the wet fields and lays its gold hand nowhere but everywhere.

Then I rise.

No lesson. No witness.

Only the wild earth under me,

and my own voice—

not asking,

not apologizing—

breaking the dark apart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem about resentment, beauty, memory, and release, moving between winter, New York City, and Colorado before rain.
counterfactuals.output:
**BAROMETER**

In winter, resentment learns architecture—  
how to brace a roof with one old sentence,  
how to glaze the stairs  
so every leaving becomes a fall.

I kept yours under my tongue,  
a small iron borough.

New York went on shining offensively:  
the taxis opening their yellow throats,  
steam lifting from the grates  
like the city dreaming itself clean.  
Beauty was everywhere  
and therefore unforgivable.

At Canal Street, memory sold me  
three counterfeit versions of you.

I wore them all.

    one said *stay*  
    one said *you imagined it*  
    one had no face, only snow

Years later, Colorado—

the mountains held their blue breath  
before rain. Even the pines  
seemed to listen inward.  
The whole sky bruised beautifully,  
that dark violet pressure  
gathering over the plains.

I thought release would be thunder,  
some courthouse in the blood  
struck open.

Instead:

a drop on the wrist,  
then another—

cold coins  
returned to no one.

I stood there until the dust changed color,  
until the road gave up its ghosts,  
until your name was only weather  
moving east.

Behind me, winter  
locked its white rooms.

Ahead, the city flickered—  
glass, siren, river,  
all those windows refusing  
to remember who looked out.

And the mountains?  
They did not forgive.

They simply let the rain  
pass through them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, image-driven free-verse poem that asks, “What does it mean to let go the envy?” and concludes with the speaker mentally sealing a man inside a box.
counterfactuals.output:
The pear tree lifts its green chandeliers  
over somebody else’s house.  
Even the wasps arrive jeweled,  
their small engines fed on sweetness  
I did not grow.

Across the fence, his laughter  
keeps striking the afternoon—  
a bright coin thrown  
again and again  
into the well of my listening.

What does it mean to let go the envy?

To loosen its blue-black feathers  
from the cage of the ribs?  
To stop polishing the window  
through which another life  
appears gold-leafed, orchard-heavy,  
untouched by frost?

I have carried comparison  
like a mouthful of nails,  
tasted iron in every kindness,  
watched his hands lift  
what mine could not keep:  
the door key, the warm loaf,  
the face turning gladly toward him.

Night comes with its bucket of ink.  
The moon hangs—an empty plate.  
I gather each glittering grievance,  
each thorn with his name on it,  
each red thread pulled taut  
between wanting and wound.

In the workshop behind my eyes  
I build a small, exact room:  
six walls of unfinished pine,  
no window, no hinge,  
only the dry scent of distance.

He stands there, still shining.

I lower the lid, press down the edges,  
and, without moving a hand,  
seal him inside the box.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
